title: AI vs ML vs DL, and the learning paradigms

steps.prompt: When a teammate says 'let's add AI', what are they actually asking you to build?
steps.sub: AI, ML, deep learning, data science — the words get used as if they're the same thing, and as a PM that confusion costs you scope and budget. By the end you'll be able to place each one on a map, name the four ways machines learn, and run a quick 'is this even an AI problem?' check before you write the spec.

steps.prompt: The map: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning, with Data Science alongside.
steps.sub: Tap each card — this is the hierarchy you'll keep in your head.

cards.b: The broad ambition: machines doing things that normally need human intelligence. A goal, not a single technique. Hand-coded rules count too.

cards.h: ML — a way to do AI
cards.b: Instead of coding rules by hand, the machine LEARNS patterns from data. Acharya scoring lesson difficulty from past attempts is ML.

cards.h: Deep Learning — ML with deep nets
cards.b: ML using multi-layer neural networks that learn the features themselves, straight from raw pixels, audio, or text. LLMs live here.
Extracting insight from data: stats, dashboards, experiments, and ML too. It OVERLAPS the others — not strictly inside the AI nesting.

steps.prompt: Tap from broadest goal to narrowest technique.
chips: Deep Learning (ML with multi-layer neural nets)
AI (machines doing things that need intelligence)
hints: Which is the big ambition, and which is one specific tool inside it?
AI is the umbrella; Deep Learning is a slice of ML, which is a slice of AI.

steps.prompt: Where does Data Science sit in this picture?

options.t: It's the innermost circle, inside Deep Learning.
It's a discipline that OVERLAPS AI/ML — sharing tools, not strictly nested inside or outside.
It's the same thing as AI, just a newer name.

steps.why: Data Science is the practice of getting insight from data — that includes plain statistics and dashboards that aren't AI at all, AND machine learning that is. So it isn't a ring inside the AI nesting; it overlaps. A churn dashboard is data science with no ML; a churn-prediction model is data science AND ML.
hints: Does every data science task involve a learning model? Think dashboards and A/B tests.
Overlapping circles, not a clean nested ring.

steps.prompt: Four ways a machine can learn.
steps.sub: Tap each card — you'll sort real products into these next.

cards.b: Labeled examples: input → known answer. The model learns to predict the label. Spam filter, churn prediction, rating a lesson's difficulty.
No labels. The model finds structure on its own — clusters, groupings, topics. Customer segmentation, discovering themes in support tickets.
A reward signal, not answers. The agent tries actions and learns which maximize reward. Our drone flight policy; a tutoring policy that picks the next question.
Raw data invents its own labels (predict the next word, the missing patch). Learns general representations. It's how LLMs get pre-trained.

steps.prompt: Sort each product into the paradigm it uses.
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin.

items.t: Spam filter trained on emails labeled spam / not-spam
Predicting which subscribers will churn next month
LMS scoring how hard a lesson is, from past pass/fail data
Grouping customers into segments nobody defined in advance
Discovering recurring topics across thousands of support tickets
The drone policy learning to fly A→B from a reward signal

hints: Is there a known right answer to copy (label), no answer at all (find structure), or a reward to chase?
Segmentation and topic discovery have no labels. The drone has a reward, not labeled answers.

steps.prompt: How does an LLM like the one behind Acharya get pre-trained?
steps.sub: Match it to the right paradigm.

options.t: Humans hand-label billions of sentences with the 'correct output' (supervised).
It predicts hidden parts of raw text — labels invented from the data itself (self-supervised).
It's given a reward each time it pleases a user, with no text to read first.

steps.why: LLMs are pre-trained self-supervised: take raw text, hide the next word, ask the model to predict it — the data is its own answer key, so no human labeling is needed at this stage. That's what makes training on the whole internet possible. (Later, reinforcement-style fine-tuning with human feedback polishes behavior, but the heavy lifting is self-supervised.)
hints: Could humans possibly hand-label the entire internet? What's the cheaper trick?
The label is 'the next word' — taken straight from the text itself.

steps.sub: Tap each card — this is why modern AI took off.

cards.b: Experts hand-crafted the 'features' — edge detectors for images, keyword lists for text. Slow, brittle, capped by human imagination.
Modern AI LEARNS the features (representations) straight from raw data. No one hand-codes what a 'cat ear' looks like — the network discovers it.
Three things lined up: cheap parallel compute (GPUs), abundant data, and better algorithms. That combo made deep representation learning practical.

steps.prompt: Is this even an AI/ML problem? Tap EVERY signal that says 'yes, ML could fit'.
steps.sub: A quick feasibility gut-check before you spec it.
chips: There's a pattern in the data a human could in principle learn
We have enough representative data to learn from
The rule is fixed and exact, like 'tax = 18% of price'
A simple heuristic would already get ~80% of the value
steps.why: ML fits when there's a learnable pattern, you have enough representative data, and occasional mistakes are tolerable. The last two are red flags AGAINST ML: a fixed exact rule ('tax = 18%') is just code — don't train a model to do arithmetic. And if a simple heuristic already gets 80% of the value, ship that first; ML is the expensive option you reach for when the heuristic stalls.
hints: Three green lights, two red flags. Which two argue for plain code instead?
Exact rules and 'a heuristic already wins' both mean: don't build a model yet.

steps.prompt: Lock it in: which framing should a PM bring to the kickoff?
steps.sub: One pulls the project in the right direction.

options.t: 'Add AI' — keep it broad so the team has freedom.
'This is a supervised problem: we have labeled churn data, ~80k accounts, and a wrong guess just triggers a retention email — low cost.'
'Use deep learning because it's the most advanced.'

steps.why: The strong framing names the paradigm (supervised), confirms there's data (~80k labeled accounts), and states the cost of being wrong (low — just an email). That tells engineering what to build and tells you it's worth doing. 'Add AI' is too vague to scope; 'use deep learning because it's advanced' picks a tool before the problem — exactly backwards.
hints: Which option names the paradigm AND the data AND the cost of an error?
Picking 'deep learning' before defining the problem is choosing a hammer before seeing the nail.

steps.sub: Not graded. Tying it to your real world is what makes it stick.

fields.label: Pick a product or feature you care about. Which paradigm fits it — supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, or self-supervised?
fields.ph: e.g. recommend next lesson → reinforcement / supervised

fields.label: Run the gut-check on it: is there a learnable pattern, enough data, and is being wrong sometimes OK — or would a simple rule do?
fields.ph: e.g. enough tagged tickets to learn from; a rule misses the long tail
